questions.q: What is an object's prototype in JavaScript?
o: A copied snapshot of properties frozen at creation time
A fallback object used when an own property is missing
A TypeScript type annotation stored next to the value
A reserved keyword that marks methods as abstract ones
questions.x: The prototype link is not a copied set of keys. If a read misses on the object, the engine looks on the prototype, then that prototype's prototype, until it finds the key or hits null.
questions.h: JavaScript does not copy prototype keys onto every object. What does it do instead when a key is not found locally?

questions.q: If obj.foo is missing, where does JavaScript look next?
o: In a hidden global map of all string keys in the process
On obj's prototype, then that prototype's prototype, and so on
In localStorage under a key made from the object identity
In the function's arguments object from the current call
questions.x: Lookup order is the object itself, then its prototype, then the next link, until a hit or null. A chain can be several objects long, such as user then roleDefaults then Object.prototype then null.
questions.h: Property search walks a linked list of objects. What is the next place after the object itself?

questions.q: An object has its own isAdmin: false and a prototype with isAdmin: true. What does obj.isAdmin return?
o: true, because prototype values always override own keys
false, because an own property wins and the chain is skipped
undefined, because duplicate keys cancel each other out
true, because Object.prototype is checked before own keys
questions.x: Own properties always win. If the object already has the key, the prototype chain is not consulted. In the example, user.isAdmin is false even though the prototype has true.
questions.h: Does the engine keep walking after it already found the key on the object itself?

questions.q: Consider these claims about property lookup. (1) A missing key is searched on the object, then its prototype. (2) The chain ends at null. (3) If nothing is found, the result is undefined. Which option is correct?
o: Only the first claim is true
Only the first two claims are true
All of these statements are true
Only the third claim is true
questions.x: Search starts on the object, walks each prototype, and stops at null. A total miss returns undefined, not an exception. That walk is ordinary JavaScript inheritance, not a copy of keys.
questions.h: Which of those three lookup rules does JavaScript actually skip?

questions.q: In user -> roleDefaults -> Object.prototype -> null, where does user.toString come from?
o: It is an own property stored directly on the user object
It is found on Object.prototype after earlier links miss it
It is copied into roleDefaults when that object is created
It is injected by the engine only when console.log is used
questions.x: user has username as an own key and isAdmin from roleDefaults. toString is not on either of those, so lookup continues and finds Object.prototype.toString. Most plain objects share that same ending link.
questions.h: username is own, isAdmin is on roleDefaults. Which remaining link in that chain still has toString?
